title: The measurement chain: from plant to number

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is that the zero screw slides the whole line and shifts every check point's error by the same amount, while the span screw tilts it and makes the error grow up the range, when you turn each screw.
interactive.title: The calibration bench
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Fourteen small screens share one picture, with Back and Continue. Five show an idea, and nine ask you to try it. On a puzzle, Why? appears after the first Check. There are no marks and no timers.

The picture. The measurement chain runs across the top as five small blocks joined by arrows: Sensor, Transducer, Transmitter, 4–20 mA signal and Display. On a phone the blocks wrap onto two rows, and no word splits. The Display block shows the reading in bar. Under its name it says the pressure it is reading at, such as "at 10 bar". Below the chain sits the calibration bench, a graph of the transmitter's line. Pressure runs along the bottom from 0 to 10 bar. The output runs up the side from 4 to 20 mA, with a little room above and below. The ideal line is dashed, from 4 mA at 0 bar to 20 mA at 10 bar. The transmitter's own line is solid. Five check points sit on the pressure axis at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100% of the range. That is 0, 2.5, 5, 7.5 and 10 bar. A Check button feeds in each check pressure in turn from the reference. At each point it drops a bead at the output the transmitter sends. A table fills one row per point. Its four columns are Point, Ideal mA, Reading mA, and Error in % of span. Any error larger than 0.5% of span shows in red. On a phone the table keeps its four narrow columns. On screens 1, 6, 8 and 13 a close-up sits between the graph and the table. It draws each check point's gap from the ideal line, in % of span, from −3.6% to +3.6%, and the transmitter's gap as a solid line. A zero error shows there as a flat line off the zero, and a span error as a slope. A gap beyond the close-up's edge is left off it.

The two screws. A Zero screw slider runs from −0.80 to +0.80 mA in steps of 0.04. It slides the whole solid line up or down. A Span screw slider runs from −0.80 to +0.80 mA in steps of 0.04. It sets how far the top end of the line sits from 20 mA. So it tilts the line about its bottom end. Beside each slider, a small drawn screw turns as the slider moves.

The three other troubles. A Noise slider runs from 0 to 1% of span in steps of 0.25. With noise on, the Check drops five repeat beads at each point. Each bead lands at random within plus or minus that much of the line. A Display step switch has three buttons: 0.01 bar, 0.1 bar and 0.5 bar. The Display block rounds its reading to that step. A Sweep button ramps the pressure slowly from 0 to 10 bar. It draws what the display shows as a trace, which is a staircase when the step is coarse. The staircase is drawn in ink, beside the line. A Direction switch has three buttons: Up, Down and Both. Going down, the bench's transmitter reads 0.16 mA high at 25, 50 and 75%. At 0 and 100% it reads the same as going up. Both shows the up beads and the down beads together. On a phone each row of three buttons wraps. Answer choices sit one under another, so no word splits.

The rule it computes. The ideal output is 4 + 1.6 × pressure, in mA. That is because 16 mA of span spread over 10 bar is 1.6 mA a bar. The transmitter sends 4 + zero + (16 + span) × pressure ÷ 10. Here zero and span are the two screw settings in mA. The error in % of span is (reading − ideal) ÷ 16 × 100. The display shows (reading − 4) ÷ 1.6 in bar, rounded to its step. Noise and the down-run gap are added to the reading before it is rounded.

Screen 1, try it. This is the opening puzzle. The screws are set to zero +0.32 mA and span 0. The Check has already run. The table reads 4.32, 8.32, 12.32, 16.32 and 20.32 mA, each +2.00% of span. The close-up shows five beads in a flat row at +2%. Both screw sliders are free. The words: "This transmitter reads high at every check point. Try the two screws. Which one puts its line back on the dashed one?" Three choices, in this order: "The zero screw"; "The span screw"; "Either one". The first is right. Each wrong choice gets its own one-line hint. Why? works it through. A right Check sets the zero screw to 0. The line lands on the dashed one, and every error reads 0.00%. The Display reads 10.20 bar at 10 bar before, and 10.00 bar after. Read: the question's words.

Screen 2, show. Both screws at 0. A Pressure slider runs from 0 to 10 bar in steps of 0.5 and opens at 5 bar. A bead rides the line at the set pressure, and each block of the chain lights in turn. The Display block reads 5.00 bar. The words: "A pressure reaches the display through a chain. A sensor feels it. A transducer makes it electrical. The transmitter sends it on as 4 to 20 mA. Here its straight line turns 0 to 10 bar into 4 to 20 mA. Each bar adds 1.6 mA to the 4 mA at the bottom. So 5 bar sends 4 + 8 = 12 mA." Read: the same words. Still: the pressure at 5 bar, the bead at 12 mA, every block lit.

Screen 3, try it, typed. Both screws at 0. A bead waits on the pressure axis at 6.25 bar, between the gridlines, and its output reads ? until Check. "The transmitter turns 0 to 10 bar into 4 to 20 mA along a straight line. What current should it send at 6.25 bar?" A field in mA. Answer 14 mA. Slips: 10 mA; 12.5 mA. Each wrong answer gets a one-line hint. Why? works it through. A right Check lifts the bead to the line at 14 mA. Read: the question's words.

Screen 4, show. Both screws at 0. A brace along the bottom reads "Range 0 to 10 bar, span 10 bar". A brace up the side reads "Span 16 mA". One small block on the line is marked "1% of span: 0.1 bar, 0.16 mA". The words: "The range runs from the lowest value an instrument is set for to the highest. Here that is 0 to 10 bar. Its span is the difference, 10 bar in and 16 mA out.[^1] Here, errors are counted in per cent of span. So 1% is 0.1 bar or 0.16 mA anywhere on the line." Read: the same words. Still: as opened, nothing to move.

Screen 5, try it, typed. The bottom axis is relabelled −1 to 9 bar, and the span brace reads "Span ?". "A transmitter is set for −1 to 9 bar. What is its span?" A field in bar. Answer 10 bar. Slips: 9 bar; 8 bar. Each wrong answer gets a one-line hint. Why? works it through. A right Check fills the brace with "Span 10 bar". Read: the question's words.

Screen 6, show. As the screen opens, a short film moves the screw sliders. The zero screw eases up to +0.48 mA and back to 0, sliding the line up and down. Then the span screw turns to −0.48 mA, tilting the line about its bottom end. Then both screws are free. The five check beads, the close-up and the table are drawn live as the screws move. The words: "The zero screw slides the whole line up or down. The span screw changes its slope.[^2] Here the span screw tilts the line about its bottom end. Slide each one and watch the beads." Read: "The zero screw slides the whole line up or down. The span screw changes its slope. Here the span screw tilts the line about its bottom end. In the picture it has tilted the line 0.48 mA low at 10 bar. At 0 bar it still reads 4 mA." Still: zero 0, span −0.48.

Screen 7, try it, typed. The screws are set to zero +0.32 mA and span 0, and both are locked. The table shows the readings. Its Error column reads ? until Check. "This transmitter reads 4.32 mA at 0 bar and 20.32 mA at 10 bar. An error that is the same at every point is a zero error. What is its error at 0 bar, in per cent of span?" A field in %. Answer 2%. Slips: 0.32%; 8%; 1.6%. Each wrong answer gets a one-line hint. Why? works it through. A right Check fills the Error column with +2.00% on every row. Read: the question's words.

Screen 8, show. The screws are set to zero 0 and span −0.48 mA. The Check runs on its own as the screen opens. The table fills: 4.00 mA, 0.00%; 7.88 mA, −0.75%; 11.76 mA, −1.50%; 15.64 mA, −2.25%; 19.52 mA, −3.00%. In the close-up the beads fall in a straight slope from 0 to −3%. The words: "A calibration feeds in known pressures at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100%. It compares each output with the ideal. This transmitter is right at 0 bar, but its error grows in step with the pressure. That is a span error, out by −3% of span at the top." Read: the same words. Still: the Check run, the table full.

Screen 9, try it, typed. The screws are set to zero 0 and span +0.40 mA, and both are locked. Only the 0 bar and 10 bar rows are filled, with 4.00 mA and 20.40 mA. The 50% row reads ?. "A transmitter reads 4.00 mA at 0 bar and 20.40 mA at 10 bar. What is its error at 50%, in per cent of span?" A field in %. Answer 1.25%. Slips: 2.5%; 0.2%; 0%. Each wrong answer gets a one-line hint. Why? works it through. A right Check fills the 50% row with 12.20 mA and +1.25%. Read: the question's words.

Screen 10, show. The graph splits into three small panels, stacked one above another. Each is a copy of the bench with both screws at 0. Panel A is Noise. Its Noise slider opens at 0.5% of span, and five beads scatter at each point. Panel B is Display step. Its step opens at 0.5 bar, and a Sweep has drawn the display's staircase in ink beside the line. Panel C is Direction. Its switch opens on Both, and the down beads sit 0.16 mA above the up beads at 25, 50 and 75%. The words: "Some trouble is not the line at all. Noise scatters repeat readings. How closely they agree is the repeatability. A coarse display rounds them onto steps. With hysteresis, the down run reads apart from the up run. The screws only move the line, so they cure none of these." Read: the same words. Still: as opened.

Screen 11, try it. Four small panels are stacked. A is the noise panel at 0.5%. B is the 0.5 bar staircase. C has the up and down beads apart. D has five tight beads at each point, all 2% high. "Which of these could the zero and span screws put right?" Four choices, in this order: "A, the readings scattered round the line"; "B, the readout climbing in steps"; "C, the up and down runs apart"; "D, the tight beads all 2% high". The fourth is right. Each wrong choice gets its own one-line hint. Why? works it through. A right Check slides D's beads down onto the dashed line. Read: the question's words.

Screen 12, try it, typed and mixed. Both screws at 0. A shaded band either side of the line shows ±0.5% of span. It is drawn 10 times wider so it can be seen. A marker sits at 1 bar. "A 0 to 10 bar transmitter has an accuracy of ±0.5% of span. No reading should be further than that from the true value. It reads 1 bar. How big can its error be, as a per cent of the reading?" A field in %. Answer 5%. Slips: 0.5%; 0.05%; 50%. Each wrong answer gets a one-line hint. Why? works it through. Read: the question's words.

Screen 13, try it, mixed. Both screws are locked at zero +0.16 mA and span −0.32 mA. The Check has already run. The table reads 4.16 mA, +1.00%; 8.08 mA, +0.50%; 12.00 mA, 0.00%; 15.92 mA, −0.50%; 19.84 mA, −1.00%. The close-up shows the gaps as a slope through zero at 5 bar. "This transmitter reads 4.16 mA at 0 bar, 12.00 mA at 5 bar and 19.84 mA at 10 bar. What should you do?" Three choices, in this order: "Pass it, because it reads right at 5 bar"; "Set the zero, then the span, then check the zero"; "Set the span, then the zero, and stop there". The second is right. Each wrong choice gets its own one-line hint. Why? works it through. A right Check eases the zero screw to 0, so 10 bar reads 19.68 mA, −2.00%. Then it eases the span screw to 0, and every error reads 0.00%. Read: the question's words.

Screen 14, try it, mixed. The Display step is set to 0.1 bar, and the Display block shows 6.3 bar. "The display steps in 0.1 bar and shows 6.3 bar. Someone logs it as 6.27 bar. Is that a fair record?" Three choices, in this order: "No. 6.3 only means nearer 6.3 than 6.2 or 6.4"; "Yes. 6.27 rounds to 6.3, so the two agree"; "Yes, as long as the pressure is held steady". The first is right. Each wrong choice gets its own one-line hint. Why? works it through. A right Check shows a closing line: "A straight line, its zero and its span. A display, a controller or a trip can trust the number only as far as that line. Next, the sensors at the start of the chain, beginning with temperature." Read: the question's words.
interactive.ignores: The 0 to 10 bar transmitter and every error on it are example values, chosen large enough to see. The reference pressure is taken as perfect. A real reference has a small error of its own. So it should be a good deal more accurate than the instrument it checks. The transmitter's line is drawn perfectly straight. A real one bends a little, and neither screw removes the errors that bend makes. Here the span screw tilts the line about its bottom end and leaves the zero alone. On many real transmitters, each screw moves the other end a little. So zero and span are set in turn and checked again. Many transmitters set zero and span from buttons or a handheld rather than screws. The effect on the line is the same. The noise is drawn as a random spread inside a fixed band. Real noise has no hard edge. The gap between the up and down runs is drawn as a fixed 0.16 mA at the three middle points. A real gap varies from instrument to instrument. The accuracy band on screen 12 is drawn 10 times wider than to scale. The bench leaves out how fast the output follows a change of pressure. It also leaves out what temperature does to the reading.

explain.text:
A reading on a screen comes at the end of a chain. Each link turns one quantity into the next. To trust the number, you check a transmitter's straight line against a standard. One adjustment slides the line, and the other tilts it.

A sensor feels the pressure in the pipe. A transducer turns what it feels into an electrical quantity. A transmitter sends that on as a current. This one is calibrated so its range gives 4 to 20 mA.[^3] At the far end, a display turns the current back into bar. The transmitter here is set for 0 to 10 bar, and its output follows a straight line. Its range is 0 to 10 bar. Those are the lowest and highest values it is set to read. Its [[span]] is the difference between the two ends.[^1] That is 10 bar on the way in and 16 mA on the way out. So each bar adds 16 ÷ 10 = 1.6 mA to the 4 mA at the bottom. 5 bar sends 4 + 8 = 12 mA. A range of −1 to 9 bar has the same 10 bar span, because 9 − (−1) = 10.

Checking that line against a standard, and setting it right, is [[calibration]]. Known pressures go in, often at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100% of the range. Each output is compared with the ideal line. Its error is worked out in per cent of span, as the error in mA ÷ 16 mA × 100. Two adjustments set the line, and they are often screws. The zero screw slides the whole line up or down. The span screw changes its slope.[^2] A slide moves every point by the same amount. So a zero error is the same size at every point. Here the span screw tilts the line about its bottom end. That leaves 0 bar where it is and moves each point in proportion to its pressure. So a span error is nothing at 0 bar. It grows in step with the pressure and is largest at 10 bar.

Say a transmitter reads 4.32 mA at 0 bar and 20.32 mA at 10 bar. Both ends are 0.32 mA high. That is 0.32 ÷ 16 × 100 = 2% of span. The same error at both ends is a zero error, and the zero screw slides it out. Another transmitter reads 4.00 mA at 0 bar but 19.52 mA at 10 bar. It is right at the bottom and 0.48 mA low at the top, which is −3% of span. That error grows up the range, so it is a span error. A calibration corrects both zero and span errors.[^4] Set the zero at the bottom first, then the span at the top. Then check the zero again. On many transmitters, each screw moves the other end a little.

Accuracy is often stated in per cent of full scale. On a 0 to 10 bar range, full scale is the same as the span. The error then stays the same size across the range, so it is a bigger share of a low reading.[^5] ±0.5% of 10 bar is ±0.05 bar anywhere on the line. At 10 bar that is 0.5% of the reading. At 1 bar it is 5%.

Not every poor reading means the line is in the wrong place. Repeat readings at one pressure can scatter round the line. A digital display rounds each reading onto its steps. Say a display steps in 0.1 bar and shows 6.3 bar. That says only that the value is nearer 6.3 than 6.2 or 6.4. So log 6.3 bar, not 6.27. Some instruments read a little differently on the way up than on the way down. That is [[hysteresis]]. The output depends on which way the input last moved. The screws move the whole line. So they cannot cure scatter, steps or hysteresis.

Accuracy is how close a reading comes to the true value.[^6] Precision is how closely a reading can be pinned down, without reference to the true value.[^7] Repeatability is how closely repeat readings agree, at the same pressure and coming from the same direction.[^8] So tight clusters of readings 2% high at every point are precise but not accurate. The zero screw puts them right. An oil pressure trip often acts on a number that comes down a chain like this. The trip can be trusted only as far as that number can. **Calibration checks an instrument's input-to-output line against a standard. The zero screw slides the line and the span screw changes its slope.[^2] So a zero error is the same at every point, and a span error grows from the bottom of the range to the top.**

analogy.text: A tape measure with a bent hook reads every length 2 mm long. That is a zero error, the same at every length. Another tape reads 1% long at every length. It is out by 10 mm over a metre and 50 mm over 5 m. That is a span error, growing with the length.
analogy.breaks: A tape has no screws, so a bad one is replaced, not set again. A tape also gives the same reading every time. A transmitter's readings can scatter from one to the next, or differ going up and coming down.

practice.text:
**Safety first:** a transmitter in service feeds a display, a controller or a trip. Its output will move while you test it. Whatever it feeds may act on that. Agree with whoever relies on the reading. Under your permit, put the loop or trip it feeds in a safe state before you isolate it from the process. Then safely vent the pressure trapped behind the isolating valve. Do that before you connect the reference.

- Note the range. Work out the span on the way in and on the way out.
- Write down the ideal output at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100% of the range.
- Feed in each pressure from a reference, going up and then coming down. Record each output.
- Work out each error in per cent of span, as (reading − ideal) ÷ output span × 100.
- The same error at every point is a zero error. An error that grows from nothing at the bottom is a span error. Set the zero at the bottom, then the span at the top. Then check the zero again.
- Up and down runs that differ are not the line. Nor are repeat readings that spread. The screws will not cure them. Record them, and compare them with the instrument's stated accuracy.
- Log a reading to the display's step, never finer.

**Rule of thumb:** on a 4 to 20 mA signal, 1% of span is 0.16 mA.

**Worked example:** a 0 to 16 bar transmitter sends 4 to 20 mA. So its line rises 1 mA a bar. It reads 4.08 mA at 0 bar. That is 0.08 mA high, or +0.5% of span. It reads 19.92 mA at 16 bar. That is 0.08 mA low, or −0.5%. At 8 bar it reads 12.00 mA, exactly right. So a check at the middle alone would pass it. Slide the zero down 0.08 mA. Now 0 bar reads 4.00 mA. But 16 bar reads 19.84 mA, which is 0.16 mA low, or −1% of span. That is a span error. So tilt the top up 0.16 mA to 20.00 mA. Then check 0 bar again.

**Common mistakes**
- Dividing the error by the reading, or by 20 mA. Divide by the 16 mA span.
- Forgetting the 4 mA at the bottom. 75% of the range is 16 mA, not 12 mA.
- Turning the span screw to cure an error that is the same at every point.
- Checking one point only. A zero error and a span error can cancel in the middle.
- Reading ±0.5% of span as ±0.5% of the reading. At a tenth of the range, it is 5% of the reading.
- Logging a reading finer than the display steps.
- Expecting a calibration to cure scatter or hysteresis.

sources.title: CALIBRATION PRINCIPLES - International Society of Automation
sources.quote: Span is defined as the algebraic difference between the upper and lower range values.

sources.title: CALIBRATION PRINCIPLES - International Society of Automation
sources.quote: The zero adjustment is used to produce a parallel shift of the input-output curve. The span adjustment is used to change the slope of the input-output curve.

sources.title: CALIBRATION PRINCIPLES - International Society of Automation
sources.quote: the engineer has determined the instrument will be calibrated for 0-to-300 psig = 4-to-20 mA

sources.title: CALIBRATION PRINCIPLES - International Society of Automation
sources.quote: Zero and span errors are corrected by performing a calibration.

sources.title: HVAC Accuracy Statements 101 - Accuspec
sources.quote: In a percentage of full-scale statement, the numeric magnitude of the error remains the same throughout the range. The percentage error goes up as the measured value goes down.

sources.title: Studio Measurement and Uncertainty Analysis
sources.quote: Accuracy is the closeness of agreement between a measured value and a true or accepted value.

sources.title: Studio Measurement and Uncertainty Analysis
sources.quote: Precision is a measure of how well a result can be determined (without reference to a theoretical or true value).

sources.title: 5.0 Terminology
sources.quote: The closeness of agreement among consecutive measurements of the output for the same value of the input under the same operating conditions and approaching from the same direction.
